title: Earning Trust in Coding Agents
subtitle: Verification, skills and agent-friendly architecture: a practitioner's study guide to Lauren Tan's Grok Bot session
learningAim: Run a small fleet of coding agents behind the controls you would demand of any production change system: admitted work, isolated workspaces, real verification, hard architectural checks, human review, and a gated promotion. Justify each control from what this talk says, and from what the simulator shows breaking without it.

talkChapters.title: Opening: agents as colleagues
talkChapters.summary: Pre-roll remarks: the goal of agents that fix bugs unattended, the engineer as a manager of agents, and a duty to keep the codebase safe for non-engineers to change.

talkChapters.title: The trust problem and the trust curve
talkChapters.summary: Screen share begins. Overconfident agents erode trust; low trust forces micromanagement, the manager parallel; a self-described unscientific chart of trust against parallelism.

talkChapters.title: From supervising to auto-merge
talkChapters.summary: Five months up the curve: agents now auto-merge and she reviews on main. A personal contribution chart and self-reported PR counts.

talkChapters.title: Verification as the core skill
talkChapters.summary: Verification means the agent runs the real app, traces and profiles. An early performance story where she, not the agent, was the verifier and bottleneck.

talkChapters.title: The control skill and the feature map
talkChapters.summary: The Control Glass skill drives the app through debugging protocols. A feature map tells agents where each feature lives and how to reach it, and handles vague bug reports.

talkChapters.title: What pstack is and how it grew
talkChapters.summary: The origin of the plugin's name. It grew one skill at a time from observed failure modes, such as agents claiming causes without reading the relevant code.

talkChapters.title: Maintaining skills with evals
talkChapters.summary: Evals as unit tests for skills: a coordinator rubric, sub-agents in disguised directories, cross-model matrices, judge models and looping to a target score. Includes a brief screen-annotation interruption. Closes on the head-chef analogy.

talkChapters.title: Start local, then cloud agents
talkChapters.summary: Build verification locally where you can watch it, then move to cloud agents. An automated bug-reproduction agent and a warning against jumping straight to huge fleets.

talkChapters.title: Recap: there is no shortcut up the curve
talkChapters.summary: The host recaps the path; she adds that trust is personal and urges forking and adapting skills rather than trusting hers blindly.

talkChapters.title: The case for rewriting greenfield code
talkChapters.summary: Big-tech guardrails already suit agents; vibe-coded greenfield apps drift without them. Covers the Grok Bot refactor and why strict CI lets non-engineers contribute.

talkChapters.title: PR size and atomic history
talkChapters.summary: No hard cap on PR size, but agents are encouraged to split work so history stays informative and reverts stay easy.

talkChapters.title: Dune: CI that bans what agents get wrong
talkChapters.summary: Bans on a React hook and on code comments; process isolation in Electron and the frame budget; dependency-graph checks between main and renderer directories.

talkChapters.title: Layers of enforcement
talkChapters.summary: Conventional, co-located feature directories; the shortest path made the right path; hard checks versus soft rules; strict compilers; repeated review comments as a smell.

talkChapters.title: Tokens, cost and ROI
talkChapters.summary: She says she works at an AI lab with effectively unlimited tokens and frames setup cost as an ROI question. Includes an aside announcing a new model release.

talkChapters.title: Non-engineers shipping through Grok Bot
talkChapters.summary: Product and design colleagues use Grok Bot's chat-style agents and ship fixes; she credits the strict architecture. Session ends.

lessons.title: Trust is the throttle on parallelism
lessons.question: Why can't I simply run more agents, and what actually lets me add them?
lessons.summary: The talk treats trust, not compute, as the limit on how many agents one person can run. Trust is earned by evidence that agents behave correctly without you watching.
practitioner: Tan opens with the problem rather than the tools. Agents that guess, invent causes and announce they have found the culprit again and again teach you to distrust them (63.1-95.1). She compares the result to managing engineers you do not trust: you end up hovering over every change (103.2-131.4).

Her hand-drawn chart, which she calls unscientific, plots this as a curve. Trust is on one axis and the number of agents on the other, marked from one up to thousands (133.2-196.4; SHOWN 52.3). At the low end you supervise one or a few agents and read every output. You cannot fan out, because spawning many agents is pointless when you do not trust the output of one (190.2-196.4). She says that over about five months she climbed the curve. She reached the point where agents merge their own PRs and she reviews what has already landed on main (198.4-232.0).

For an operator this is a familiar shape. You do not raise a deployment's replica count until its readiness probe actually means something. Here, adding agents is safe only after something other than your eyes can tell good output from bad. She also warns against skipping the climb: jumping to hundreds of cloud agents mostly burns tokens (1639.9-1657.3).

Treat her numbers as one person's self-report under unusual conditions. She mentions around a thousand PRs in a month and about 800 by the twelfth of the next (292.3-315.6). She also expects listeners to question how good that code is (315.6-329.4). A slide shown at the same time claims more than 3000 PRs in five months, next to a contribution chart labelled with a commit count. PRs and commits are different units, and we do not reconcile them (SHOWN 257.6). The transferable claim is the ordering, not the volume.
basics: An agent here means a language model that can run tools, such as editing files, running commands or opening a browser, in a loop until it decides it is done. Its confident tone tells you nothing about whether it is right.
Auto-merge means a change lands on the main branch without a person approving it first. Review happens afterwards, if at all.
deep: Model the curve as a control loop whose gain you raise only as your measurement improves. Without a trustworthy sensor (verification), raising gain (agent count) amplifies error; you just see it later. The talk's later sections are all about improving that sensor.

Note what she does not claim. She does not offer an error rate for the auto-merged PRs, and the 20-PRs-overnight figure (222.2-232.0, repeated at 2099.2-2106.1) is an anecdote. If you adopt auto-merge, define your own escaped-defect measure first; for example, reverts per landed change, measured by you.
analogyBreaks: Replicas of a service are identical; agent runs are not, because the same task can produce a different change each time.
A failing pod usually fails loudly. A failing agent often reports success, which is the whole trust problem.
Human trust in an engineer accumulates in that person. Agent trust lives mostly in your skills, checks and architecture, and resets when you change models or repositories.

lessons.title: Verification closes the loop
lessons.question: What does it mean for an agent to verify its own work, and why does that matter more than code quality?
lessons.summary: Verification means the agent exercises the real system as a user or profiler would. Without it, you become the verifier and the bottleneck.
practitioner: Tan names verification as the most important skill to give agents (346.0-360.4). She means real execution: running the code, capturing CPU traces or heap snapshots, driving an iOS simulator, using the product the way users do (360.4-382.7). Her careful claim is that verification does not make agents write good code; it makes them write correct code, and that is the step that earns trust (382.7-398.5).

Her early performance story shows the alternative (439.9-551.3). New to the codebase and under deadline, she captured traces by hand and passed screenshots to an agent. It confidently named a cause, and fixing it did not solve the problem. In that workflow the human runs the build, spots the failure and pastes errors back. You are the loop's sensor, so nothing parallelises (522.4-555.9).

Operations translation: an agent that only edits code is an actuator with no feedback. Verification gives each agent its own probe, so that 'done' means the system was observed in the target state, the same standard as a reconciliation loop comparing observed with desired state. Her later evals section (lesson 4) is the next layer: checking that the verification itself works.

Practical rule for adoption: an agent may not report a task done without attaching evidence from running the thing. That evidence is a test run, a trace, a screenshot from automation or a command output. 'I changed the code that should fix it' is a hypothesis, not a result.
basics: A trace is a recording of what a program did over time, often shown as a flame graph where wide blocks used the most time. A heap snapshot records memory in use.
A simulator or debugging protocol lets software click, type and measure inside an application the way a person would.
deep: Distinguish three claims an agent can make. Proposed: here is a change. Plausible: the change matches the described symptom. Verified: the symptom was reproduced, then shown absent after the change, using the same probe. Most agent overconfidence lives in the gap between plausible and verified. Make your check harness reproduce the failure before the fix, or you only test that something runs.

Verification has its own failure modes: probes that always pass, environments that differ from production, flaky measurements. Treat a verifier like a monitoring check. Prove it fires on a known-bad case before trusting its green.
analogyBreaks: A readiness probe is written by you. An agent may write or edit its own check, so it can quietly weaken the verification it reports.
Correct is not the same as maintainable; she says so directly, which is why the architecture lessons exist.

lessons.title: Control skills and feature maps: giving agents a map of the product
lessons.question: How does an agent find the feature a vague bug report is about, and reach it in the running app?
lessons.summary: The ability to drive the app is not enough; agents also need a maintained map from user-visible features to UI paths, shortcuts, selectors and code.
practitioner: Her first skill, Control Glass, drives the agents window through the Chrome DevTools Protocol. She says the window is internally called Glass, and she notes that Apple tooling plays a similar role for iOS (556.9-601.9). The skill's documentation, shown on screen, describes driving a running development build over that protocol with Playwright, including separate worktree-isolated instances (SHOWN 440.0). She says the code itself is unremarkable and an agent can write one for you (570.6-578.9).

Once agents could run the app, they still did not know the app. A report about a laggy sidebar or a broken PR tab left agents searching code and clicking aimlessly (623.4-677.7). Her fix was a feature map file shipped with the skill. It describes each feature from the user's side: where it is, how to reach it, keyboard shortcuts, and the DOM attributes used to select it through the protocol (606.7-626.3, 769.8-804.4). The README on screen calls the map the maintained verification source for the app (SHOWN 620.0).

The map's payoff is triage of poor input. Internal feedback often arrives as a screenshot plus question marks, and with the map an agent can locate the feature anyway (724.9-771.2). pstack, she says, includes a skill to create such a verification setup, including an initial map built by exploring the code, and another to maintain it (692.9-718.9, 804.4-813.5).

Operations translation: this is a service catalog or runbook index for a UI. On-call engineers with a good catalog resolve 'the dashboard is slow' quickly. Without one they search. And like a catalog, a stale map misleads, which is why maintenance is a separate, named skill.
basics: DOM attributes are labels on page elements that automation uses to find a button or panel reliably.
A skill, in this talk, is mostly a markdown file of instructions that an agent loads for a kind of task (963.8-972.4).
deep: Make the map checkable. Every entry should name a selector or path that a script can resolve, so CI can flag entries that no longer exist. A map you cannot test drifts silently, which is the same failure as an undocumented runbook.
The map is also a context-budget tool. Pointing the agent at the right files and UI path replaces open-ended searching, which spends tokens and invites wrong guesses.
analogyBreaks: A service catalog is read by people who ask when unsure; agents act on stale entries without hesitation.
UI paths change with every redesign far more often than service endpoints do.

lessons.title: pstack: skills grown from failures, tested with evals
lessons.question: Where do good agent skills come from, and how do I know a skill still works after I change it?
lessons.summary: pstack started as individual skills, each written after watching a specific agent failure. Changes are tested with evals, which are unit tests for agent behaviour, run across models and judged independently.
practitioner: pstack is Tan's plugin, a bundle of skills reflecting her engineering practices. She explains the name as a joke, a riff on another engineer's similarly named plugin, and says she never set out to build it (824.6-875.0). It accreted from individual skills, starting with the control skill (871.1-886.6).

Her method is observation. Early on she read the agent's tool calls and saw it assert a cause without ever opening the code she expected it to inspect (906.2-930.1). Each such failure mode became a skill: go read the code, stop guessing (1011.0-1035.2). She frames a skill as onboarding a strong coder who has no business context, and as markdown that steers the model with better starting context (942.8-1004.6).

Maintenance uses evals. She describes them as unit tests for agents that need no special framework (1084.5-1098.4), and pstack includes an eval playbook (1137.6-1144.2). Her process works like this:
- A coordinator agent writes a rubric and spawns sub-agents in directories named so they cannot tell they are being tested. She says agents act differently when they suspect a test (1151.7-1184.0).
- She runs the eval across several models (1196.6-1216.2).
- A judge agent from a different model cross-checks scoring (1320.0-1338.0).
- A loop repeats until the rubric is met (1338.0-1353.7).
She reruns evals whenever she modifies a skill (1218.1-1228.7). She calls maintenance hard: it requires close, critical observation, like an active pairing partner (1229.6-1287.2).

Operations translation: a skill is configuration that changes system behaviour, so changes need tests, canaries and review like any config. Evals are your regression suite. Running across models is a compatibility matrix. A different-model judge is separation of duties: the component under test does not grade itself.
basics: A plugin here is a package of skills and settings you install into an agent tool.
A rubric is a written list of what a good result must include, used to score attempts consistently.
deep: Looping on a score invites overfitting: the skill learns the rubric, not the job. Keep a held-out set of tasks the loop never sees, and track at least one outcome that cannot be argued with, such as tests passing in a clean checkout.

Disguising eval directories addresses evaluation awareness. In your own setup, also isolate side effects: eval runs belong in disposable worktrees or containers with no credentials, so a test agent cannot touch anything real.
Pin what you evaluated: model identifier, skill commit, tool versions. An eval result without that context, like a load test without the build ID, cannot be reproduced.
analogyBreaks: Unit tests are deterministic; eval runs are sampled, so a single pass proves little and you need repetitions.
A config change has bounded effects; a skill wording change can alter behaviour on tasks it never mentions.

lessons.title: Agent-friendly architecture: make the shortest path the right path
lessons.question: How can a codebase stop agents from producing plausible but harmful changes before any human reads them?
lessons.summary: Agents copy patterns and take shortcuts. Dune, the architecture behind Grok Bot, turns lessons into hard CI failures and conventional structure, leaving soft rules as backup only.
practitioner: Tan argues that established big-company codebases already suit agents. They were built around guardrails, conventions and restricted credentials so the least experienced contributor cannot cause damage (1879.2-1970.7). The risk is greenfield code written quickly by agents with nobody reading it. With no guardrails, agents solve each task by the most convenient route until the codebase spirals (1971.0-2071.9). She describes a refactor of Grok Bot onto a new architecture of over 600 PRs (2103.6-2124.4). After it, she says, she no longer reads the code (2124.4-2138.2).

Dune is described as something like Next.js for Electron apps, designed for agents to write (2346.3-2389.5). It encodes lessons as CI failures. Examples:
- A React hook that commonly causes bugs is banned (2352.8-2399.9).
- Code comments are banned because agents fill them with stale, misattributed history (2404.1-2441.4).
- Electron main and renderer code live in separate directories, and a dependency-graph check fails any import across the boundary (2499.6-2587.8).
The reason for the boundary is concrete: work leaking onto the renderer competes with a frame budget of about 16 ms, causing jank and long tasks (2525.2-2559.5). She says the existing agents window lacks this isolation and regresses often (2462.7-2499.6). The Dune page shown on screen treats agent habits, such as copying the nearest pattern, as design inputs. One of its five rules is that forbidden dependencies fail mechanically (SHOWN 2700.0).

She describes layers of enforcement and shows them as a handwritten list: codebase, then static analysis, then rules and Bugbot, then skills, then a style guide (SHOWN 2605.0).
- The strongest is conventional structure: each feature lives in one directory, because agents copy existing patterns (2618.9-2684.8).
- Her principle is to make the shortest path the best path, since agents take shortcuts anyway (2695.8-2715.6).
- Static analysis, lint and compiler diagnostics fail CI. Rules, skills and the AI review bot she calls Bugbot are soft, because agents forget them (2761.4-2819.8).
- She points to strict compilers as a source of trust (2823.9-2869.4).
- She treats a repeated human review comment as a smell: turn it into a lint rule or a CI failure, or remove the possibility entirely (2869.4-2911.2).

Operations translation: this is admission control for code. Policy-as-code rejects a pod that runs as root; the review comment 'please don't run as root' would not. Network segmentation is the main and renderer import boundary. Soyspray already lives this way, with NetworkPolicy, non-root images and digest promotion. The lesson is to apply the same reflex to the code agents write.
basics: CI is the automated pipeline that runs checks on every proposed change and can block it.
Lint rules are automated style and safety checks that flag known-bad patterns.
An Electron app has a main process and a renderer process that draws the UI; heavy work in the renderer makes the UI stutter.
deep: Rank every invariant by enforcement strength: impossible by construction, then compile error, then CI failure, then review-bot warning, then written rule. Push each one as high as is affordable. Anything enforced only by written rules will eventually be violated at agent volume.

Encoding is not free. Every hard rule needs a clear failure message telling an agent how to fix it, or agents will work around the check, for example by moving code to dodge an import rule. Review the workarounds as seriously as the rules.
Bans like no comments are local choices with tradeoffs, made for her codebase. Copy the method of observing a recurring agent failure and making it unrepresentable, not the specific bans.
analogyBreaks: Admission policies govern a small, stable schema; code-level rules must anticipate creative violations by an agent optimising to pass.
A human intern learns the reason behind a guardrail; an agent mostly learns only that the check fails.

lessons.title: Operating the fleet: local first, cloud agents, small atomic PRs
lessons.question: Once verification exists, how do agents pick up work and land it safely at volume?
lessons.summary: Build and watch verification locally, then let cloud agents act on signals such as bug reports. Keep changes small and revertible, and promote only through hard gates.
practitioner: Asked where to start, Tan says to start locally, where you can watch the agent operate the app and its interfaces (1467.7-1503.1). She herself mostly uses cloud agents. She argues that verification skills pay off team-wide once agents run remotely (1505.7-1548.4).

Her example is an internal agent she calls Benny. It takes incoming bug reports, runs the app on its own cloud machine with the same control skills, and tries to reproduce the issue. In one case it reproduced a bug that was already fixed on the main branch, so the answer was just to ship a build (1554.5-1617.9). Its message on screen says the bug reproduced on the prior commit and is gone on the fix (SHOWN 1584.8). That is verification used for triage, not only for fixes. The host's recap orders the path as verification, local trust, cloud agents responding to signals, then auto-merge, and she agrees (1658.2-1713.6).
On PR size there is no hard cap. Agents are encouraged to split work. She values a history in which each PR describes one small change that is easy to revert and to bisect (2277.7-2325.5).

Two unnarrated screens bear on the human gate:
- An agent's working notes name one human approval from a security or build review group as the last dependency before merging, with no bot route (SHOWN 411.9).
- A later panel reports that merge attempts were refused while that review was pending (SHOWN 2240.0).
Our read: even at the top of her curve, some changes still wait for a person, and the tooling refuses rather than bypasses.
basics: A cloud agent runs on a remote machine rather than your laptop, so it can work while you are away.
A git worktree is a second working directory attached to the same repository, letting several agents edit in parallel without overwriting each other.
deep: Retries in agent pipelines are not idempotent by default: re-sending a bug report can spawn a second agent and a second PR. Key each task by a stable identifier, such as report ID plus repository, and make claiming atomic.
Reproduction before fixing doubles as deduplication: if the issue does not reproduce on main, the right output is a note, not a PR. Her Benny example shows this outcome.

The host asks about worktrees and isolated sub-agents (1431.5-1464.5). The spoken answer is practical advice, not an isolation design. The only isolation detail is on screen: the control skill's documentation describes worktree-isolated instances (SHOWN 440.0), and she does not narrate it. Treat everything else about isolation as our recommendation.
analogyBreaks: Queue consumers process identical message types; agent tasks vary widely and some cannot be finished.
Kubernetes rollouts can be undone automatically; a merged bad change needs a revert PR and someone to notice.

docs.title: git-worktree manual (git 2.56.0)
docs.note: The talk does not describe how agents are isolated; this page documents the mechanism the lab uses. One repository can have several working trees, each with its own HEAD and index, sharing everything else. By default, git refuses to check out a branch in a new worktree while another worktree holds it. Removing a worktree with uncommitted or untracked changes requires force, and prune clears records of worktrees deleted by hand.

lessons.title: Cost, leverage and deciding for yourself
lessons.question: Is this worth it without unlimited tokens, and what should I adopt first?
lessons.summary: She is candid that her token budget is unusual and frames setup as an ROI question. The cheap, transferable parts are verification and hard checks; volume comes last.
practitioner: Asked whether this is realistic on a normal budget, Tan says she works at an AI lab with effectively unlimited tokens, so her approach should not be copied wholesale, though she thinks it can be done without breaking the bank (2973.8-2992.4). She frames it as ROI: setup and refactoring consume many tokens up front, in exchange for a codebase where even weaker agents do good work, and for being able to enforce constraints one person could never maintain alone (3000.3-3126.8).

She credits the strict architecture with letting product managers and designers ship fixes through Grok Bot's chat-style interface, which she likens to a messaging app with named agents (3271.0-3402.4). During the session she also announced a new model release: a Grok model numbered 4.6 that she believed kept the previous per-token price. She hedged that statement herself (3149.5-3192.6). Treat it as time-sensitive. The Grok Bot overview captured on 2026-10-11 already links a later model version.

For a home cluster the order matters more than the scale. First, require verification evidence for every agent task. Second, convert repeated review comments into checks. Third, add isolation and claims for parallel work. Only then consider unattended agents, and keep the promotion boundary human.
basics: Tokens are the units that model usage is billed in; long contexts and many parallel agents multiply them.
deep: Estimate cost per verified, merged change rather than per agent run: wasted runs, failed verifications and duplicates are all cost. The simulator's abstract cost units let you see how gates shift spending from rework to checks.
analogyBreaks: Infrastructure cost is predictable per resource; agent cost varies with task difficulty and failure loops.

glossary.plain: Her informal picture of moving from watching every agent step to letting agents work unattended.
glossary.practitioner: Parallelism is gated by how much evidence you have that output is correct.
glossary.deep: Raise loop gain only as sensor quality improves.

glossary.plain: The agent checks its work by running the real app.
glossary.practitioner: Real execution, traces, profiling or simulation; yields correct, not necessarily good, code.
glossary.deep: Reproduce the symptom before the fix, observe it absent after, with the same probe.

glossary.plain: A written instruction file an agent loads for a type of task.
glossary.practitioner: Mostly markdown encoding context and procedure; born from observed failures.
glossary.deep: Configuration that changes behaviour; version, test and review it.

glossary.plain: Lets an agent drive and inspect the running app.
glossary.practitioner: Uses debugging protocols such as Chrome DevTools Protocol, or Apple simulator tooling.
glossary.deep: The actuator-and-sensor half of a verification loop.

glossary.plain: A guide telling agents where each feature is and how to reach it.
glossary.practitioner: Location, navigation, shortcuts and selector attributes for each feature.
glossary.deep: Make entries machine-checkable to catch drift.

glossary.plain: Tan's plugin of skills, named partly as a joke.
glossary.practitioner: Includes skills for creating and maintaining verification setups and an eval playbook, per the talk.
glossary.deep: The pinned README, captured 2026-10-11, lists create and maintain verification skills and an eval playbook. Transcript spellings vary; the slide at 340 shows pstack.

glossary.plain: A test of whether an agent with a skill behaves as intended.
glossary.practitioner: Unit tests for agents; rubric, sub-agents, multiple models, independent judge.
glossary.deep: Sampled, not deterministic; use repetitions and held-out tasks.

glossary.plain: A second agent that scores the first one's work.
glossary.practitioner: She uses a different model to reduce bias.

glossary.plain: An agent working on a remote machine.
glossary.practitioner: Can act on signals such as bug reports without you present.
glossary.deep: Needs isolation, scoped credentials and idempotent task claims.

glossary.plain: Changes land without prior human approval.
glossary.practitioner: She reviews after landing; only advisable behind hard checks.
glossary.deep: Never apply to the cluster promotion boundary.

glossary.plain: Code name for the agent-oriented architecture behind Grok Bot.
glossary.practitioner: Conventional feature directories plus CI bans on known-bad patterns.
glossary.deep: She presents it as a set of ideas and principles, not a planned open-source release (2720.9-2724.9).

glossary.plain: Checks that block versus advice that can be ignored.
glossary.practitioner: CI, lint and compiler errors block; rules, skills and review bots can be forgotten.
glossary.deep: Push each invariant to the strongest affordable layer.

glossary.plain: The two halves of an Electron app; the renderer draws the UI.
glossary.practitioner: Heavy work in the renderer causes stutter; CI blocks crossing imports.
glossary.deep: About 16 ms per frame at 60 fps.

glossary.plain: An extra working folder on the same repository.
glossary.practitioner: Lets parallel agents edit without overwriting each other.
glossary.deep: By default, git will not check out a branch that another worktree already holds (DOCS git 2.56.0, retrieved 2026-10-11). In the lab, each stub agent gets its own worktree and branch, so a clash shows up as a merge conflict.

simulator.title: Two agents, one file
simulator.predictionQuestion: Agents A and B both edit config line 1 in a shared working tree. What happens to A's change?
choices: A's edit is silently overwritten by B
simulator.explanation: In a shared tree the last writer wins with no signal. With per-agent worktrees the same edits surface as a merge conflict at integration, where a reviewer sees them.
simulator.expectedContract: shared: tick 3 A writes, tick 4 B overwrites, event lost_update(T1), merged=1, wasted=1. worktree: tick 5 merge_conflict(T1,T2), routed to review, lost_update=0. Golden logs per mode.

simulator.title: Done, or verified?
simulator.predictionQuestion: Three agent reports say 'fixed'. One change does not fix the symptom. With the verification gate off, how many fixes reach main?
simulator.explanation: Without a probe that reproduces the symptom, self-reports are accepted. With the gate on, task T3 fails reproduction-after and returns to the queue. Illustrative outcome, not a measured rate.
simulator.expectedContract: off: merged=3, defects_reaching_main=1 (T3), detection deferred. on: verify_fail(T3) at tick 4, retry, merged=2 plus T3 pending, defects_reaching_main=0, extra cost=3 verify units. T3's outcome is a scripted event, not a probability.

simulator.title: The reviewer is the bottleneck
simulator.predictionQuestion: Four agents produce 12 PRs; one reviewer clears 2 per tick. Hard checks catch 4 of the PRs automatically. What changes?
choices: The review queue shrinks because checks reject 4 before review
simulator.explanation: Adding agents without automated gates only grows the human queue. Converting review comments into checks removes scripted bad PRs before review.
simulator.expectedContract: agents=4, checks off: queue peaks at 10, last review at tick 6. Checks on: 4 auto-rejected, queue peak 6, last review at tick 4. Deterministic schedule; not a throughput prediction.

simulator.title: Retry without a claim
simulator.predictionQuestion: A bug report is delivered twice after a timeout. With naive retry, how many PRs appear?
simulator.explanation: Each delivery spawns its own agent and branch. With an atomic claim keyed by report ID, the second delivery logs skip_already_claimed.
simulator.expectedContract: naive: PR-a and PR-b for R7, wasted=3 units, reviewer sees a duplicate. idempotent: claim(R7) at tick 1, skip at tick 3, PRs=1.

simulator.title: The shortcut import
simulator.predictionQuestion: An agent's quickest fix imports heavy main-process code into the renderer. With the boundary check on, where is it caught?
choices: At review only if the reviewer notices
simulator.explanation: Hard checks fail the build. With soft rules only, catching it depends on the reviewer; the scenario scripts the reviewer missing it, to illustrate the gap, not as a measured miss rate.
simulator.expectedContract: soft: C1 merged, event boundary_violation_in_main, later jank_report(tick 8). ci: ci_fail(C1, import_boundary) at tick 2, agent revises via the allowed path, merged clean.

lab.title: Preflight and ownership
lab.goal: Create an owned, disposable lab root that the script refuses to leave.
steps: Download lab.py into a directory of its own, outside any repository, and read it before running it. It uses only the Python standard library, opens no network connection and never runs a shell string. It does not look for credentials because it needs none.
Choose a lab root whose parent already exists and which does not exist yet, for example ~/agent-lab. The script refuses your home directory itself and the filesystem root.
Run: python3 -I lab.py run --root ~/agent-lab

Before writing anything, the script checks the root and every parent for symlinks and for Git repositories that have a remote. Only then does it create the root with mode 0700 and an ownership marker that records the path and your user ID.
The same run continues through every later exercise, using deterministic stub agents only. Each exercise below explains one printed line.
lab.expected: First line: PREFLIGHT: owned root; no symlinks or Git remotes; stub agents only. The run ends with a JSON summary in which offline is true and seven steps are listed. A refusal prints a line starting with STOP: on stderr, exits with status 1 and creates nothing.
lab.failureVariant: Point --root at a new folder inside a clone that has a remote, or at your home directory. The script prints STOP and creates nothing. Point it at an existing folder it did not create, and it also stops, because the ownership marker is missing.
lab.transfer: Equivalent to a fresh, uncredentialed workspace; agents never get your kube context or registry tokens.
lab.cleanup: Nothing to clean up yet. Rerunning run resets only the scratch repository inside the owned root. Final removal is in the last exercise.

lab.title: Shared tree versus worktrees
lab.goal: See a silent lost update become a visible conflict.
steps: Printed line: WORKTREES. The script creates two worktrees, wt-a and wt-b, on branches agent-a and agent-b. Each stub agent commits a different greeting to config.txt.
It merges agent-a into main, then attempts agent-b. Git reports a conflict on config.txt. The script confirms that config.txt is the only unmerged file, then aborts the merge.
It resets main to the initial commit, so later exercises start from the verified baseline rather than from either agent's greeting.
Inspect: git -C ~/agent-lab/repo worktree list
Inspect: git -C ~/agent-lab/repo log --oneline --all
lab.expected: Results entry: CONFLICT-SURFACED: config.txt. The worktree list shows the main checkout plus wt-a and wt-b. Each agent's commit stays on its own branch, and neither is on main.
lab.verify: git -C ~/agent-lab/repo log --oneline main (lab commits only, no agent greeting commit)
lab.failureVariant: Contrast this with a shared tree. If both stubs had written config.txt in one directory, the second write would have replaced the first with no error. Worktrees turn that silent loss into a conflict a reviewer must resolve.
lab.transfer: Each Soyspray agent task gets its own worktree and branch; conflicts surface at PR review.
lab.cleanup: Nothing to clean up per exercise. The final cleanup removes the whole owned root.

lab.title: A check that runs the real thing
lab.goal: Reject a plausible but wrong change with a check that runs the app.
steps: Printed line: VERIFICATION. The script commits check.sh, which runs app.sh and passes only if the printed value is hi.
Known-good case: on main, sh check.sh prints PASS.

Known-bad case: on branch agent-c, a stub agent changes the greeting and writes a commit message claiming the fix is done. On that branch check.sh prints nothing and exits 1, and the script requires that failure.
The script switches back to main.
Inspect: git -C ~/agent-lab/repo log --oneline -1 agent-c, then git -C ~/agent-lab/repo show agent-c:config.txt
lab.expected: Results entry: PASS baseline; REJECT claimed but wrong change. The agent-c commit message claims a fix, but its config.txt reads greeting=hey.
lab.verify: (cd ~/agent-lab/repo && sh check.sh) prints PASS on main
lab.failureVariant: This one is built in. If check.sh ever passed on agent-c, the run would stop with STOP. A check that cannot fail on a known-bad change proves nothing.
lab.transfer: Soyspray CI and harness checks are the probe; require their output, not an agent's claim.
lab.cleanup: Nothing to clean up per exercise. The final cleanup removes the whole owned root.

lab.title: A checkable feature map
lab.goal: Write a map whose entries a script can validate.
steps: Printed line: FEATURE MAP. The script writes feature-map.txt with three entries, each mapping a feature name to a path: greeting to config.txt, app to app.sh, and billing to billing.sh.
It checks every listed path. Known-good: config.txt and app.sh exist. Known-bad: billing.sh is deliberately missing, and the script requires exactly that one stale entry.
The map stays untracked, so it never enters a commit.
Inspect: cat ~/agent-lab/repo/feature-map.txt
lab.expected: Results entry: STALE: billing.sh; real paths exist.
lab.verify: git -C ~/agent-lab/repo status --short (feature-map.txt is listed as untracked)
lab.failureVariant: This one is built in. If the check found no stale entry, or flagged a real path, the run would stop with STOP.
lab.transfer: A Soyspray map from app name to apps/NAME/app, manifests and checks, validated in CI.
lab.cleanup: Nothing to clean up per exercise. The final cleanup removes the whole owned root.

lab.title: Make the shortcut fail
lab.goal: Enforce an architectural boundary as a hard check.
steps: Printed line: BOUNDARY. The script creates main/heavy.sh and renderer/view.sh, then writes check-boundary.py, which fails if any renderer script refers to main/.
Known-good case: while the renderer only draws, the check prints PASS-boundary and exits 0.
Known-bad case: the stub agent takes the shortcut and makes the renderer source the main script. The check prints FAIL-boundary and exits 1, and the script requires that failure.
Inspect: cat ~/agent-lab/repo/renderer/view.sh
lab.expected: Results entry: PASS allowed path; BLOCKED shortcut import. The renderer file still contains the shortcut line, left in place so you can see what was blocked.
lab.verify: (cd ~/agent-lab/repo && python3 -I check-boundary.py) prints FAIL-boundary and exits 1, because the shortcut is still present
lab.failureVariant: Imagine replacing the check with a README sentence asking agents not to import main: nothing would stop the shortcut. The script deliberately does not include that soft-rule version.
lab.transfer: Equivalent to Soyspray's policy gates: non-root, read-only, no egress, enforced rather than requested.
lab.cleanup: Nothing to clean up per exercise. The final cleanup removes the whole owned root.

lab.title: Claim tasks atomically
lab.goal: Prevent duplicate work when a task is delivered twice.
steps: Printed line: RETRY. The script creates claims/ in the lab root, then claims report R7 by creating the directory claims/R7. Creating a directory either succeeds or fails as one operation, so only one delivery can win.
A second delivery of R7 tries to create the same directory, fails because it already exists, and is skipped. If that second claim ever succeeded, the script would stop with STOP.
No branch or worktree is opened for R7; the exercise isolates the claim itself.
Inspect: ls ~/agent-lab/claims
lab.expected: Results entry: claimed:R7 then skip:R7; one claim. ls shows a single entry, R7.
lab.failureVariant: Without a claim, each delivery would start its own agent and branch, and the reviewer would receive two PRs for one report. The simulator's retry scenario shows that version.
lab.transfer: Key agent work by report or issue ID and claim it atomically before any agent starts; a re-sent signal must not open a second PR.
lab.cleanup: Nothing to clean up per exercise. The final cleanup removes the whole owned root.

lab.title: Rehearse the promotion boundary
lab.goal: Keep activation a separate, human-approved change.
steps: Printed line: PROMOTION. The script creates branch promote from main and commits only promotion.json, which records a stub image digest and that human approval is required.
It returns to main and confirms that promotion.json is the only file that differs between main and promote. Source and activation never travel together.
The run writes results.json in the lab root, then runs verify itself. Verify rechecks ownership, the seven recorded steps, check.sh PASS on main and the promotion-only diff.
Inspect: git -C ~/agent-lab/repo diff --name-only main promote --
No step contacts a model, registry, cluster or remote. This lab has no real-model step.
lab.expected: Results entry: promotion.json only; source main unchanged. The diff command prints exactly promotion.json, and verify prints the same seven-step JSON summary.
lab.failureVariant: This one is built in. If promote differed from main by anything besides promotion.json, the run would stop with STOP. A branch that mixes a source change with the activation pin is exactly what a separate promotion PR prevents.
lab.transfer: Source PR, then CI builds the image, then a separate digest promotion PR, then Argo. No agent pushes, merges a promotion or touches the cluster.
lab.cleanup: python3 -I lab.py cleanup --root ~/agent-lab. It rechecks the ownership marker, deletes only that root, and prints that it removed the owned lab root. Then delete lab.py yourself.

adoptionPrompts: Which agent tasks will require attached verification evidence, and what counts as evidence for each?
Which review comments have I written more than twice, and what check will replace each one?
Which invariant will I make impossible by construction first?
How will each agent get an isolated workspace, and how are tasks claimed so a retry cannot duplicate work?
Which credentials, contexts and networks must an agent never see? How do I prove they cannot?
Where does agent autonomy stop: branch, PR, merge, or never beyond PR? Why?
The digest promotion stays human. Who approves it, and what must they check?
How will I measure escaped defects, for example reverts per landed change, before raising agent count?
What is my monthly token budget, and what cost per verified merged change is acceptable?
When I change a skill or model, what eval or rerun confirms behaviour did not regress?
contentCautions: The wrapper's '21+ GrokBot agents' framing does not appear in this recording, spoken or shown. The nearest spoken figure is about 20 PRs landed overnight (222.2-232.0, 2099.2-2106.1). Do not state 21+ agents anywhere.

Product spelling has four sources:
- ASR renders the name as one word, plus garbled variants; reviewed corrections normalise those to the ASR form.
- The wrapper post spells it GrokBot.
- The docs captured 2026-10-11 spell it Grok Bot.
- At 409.3 a chat channel name reads grok-bot-playground, a lowercase hyphenated slug.
The slug is consistent with two words but does not settle display spelling. Authored text uses the docs spelling, labelled as dated docs.
pstack: the slide at 340 shows pstack in lower case. ASR variants PSAC and PSAP are corrected in the transcript; PStack is left as a case variant.
Review bot: the handwritten list at 2605 shows rules/bugbot, so the ASR forms 'bug bots' and 'Bagua' are corrected to Bugbot.

Earlier guidance called 'SpaceX AI' at about 3185 a likely recognition error. That is withdrawn. The on-screen lower third reads SpaceXAI, so the phrase plausibly matches speech. Neither the phrase nor the caption is used to infer employer or role.

Role and employer: the lower third shows 'Software engineer | SpaceXAI'. In speech she says she joined Cursor about five months before (434.6-436.5) and that she works at an AI lab (2975.5-2979.7). We report both as attributed and do not reconcile them.
'fable size' at about 3115-3124 remains UNCLEAR. A model-picker label reading Fable 5 is visible on screen at 411.9 and 606.7, so the phrase may name a model. We do not interpret it.
On-screen documents call the application Sand (project list at 411.9; Dune page at 2620 onward), while speech names Grok Bot. Not reconciled.

Mode naming conflicts: the speech says 'potato mode' (1137.4-1141.0), the skill on screen is titled Lauren Mode (411.9), and the README says poteto-mode. The name is unresolved; present only what each source says.
The model release and pricing remarks (3149.5-3192.6) are dated and hedged by the speaker. Present them only as said, and point to current docs.
PR counts, the five-month timeline and the 600-PR refactor are self-reported anecdotes. The slide's '3000+ PRs in 5 months' and the chart's commit count use different units and are not reconciled.

The recording date is unknown. Relative remarks ('the 12th' 300.5-307.1, 'launched yesterday' 1995.6, 'calculated yesterday' 2103.6) are relative to the recording. Dates visible on screen, such as an attachment file name and chart axis labels, are not used to date the recording.
Speakers: ASR hears a name at 242.8 and 343.7. It is not confirmed by any frame, so use 'host'. An unseen participant draws on the shared screen around 678-682 and 1104-1130.
The burned-in animated captions are third-party machine captions; they also misspell pstack at 700. They corroborate timing only and are never spelling evidence.
She mentions another public figure's similarly named plugin when explaining pstack's name. Omit the person from lessons; it is not needed for learning.
Docs entries are dated captures. The git worktree and Grok Build pages were captured as titles only, so they are classified silent and must not be quoted.
Do not use summaries of other talks by the speaker; every number and chapter must come from this recording.
The last segment ends at 3411.65 s against 3412.10 s of audio. The 0.44 s tail is preserved as an UNCLEAR gap in provenance.
The machine transcript is not human-certified. Reviewed corrections v1 cover only the records listed in the changelog.
